messages.subject: ggplot2 geom_boxplot in polar coordinates: 0-180 direction not vertical
messages.subject_clean: ggplot2 geom_boxplot in polar coordinates: 0-180 direction not vertical
messages.body_plain:
I make a circular boxplot of element concentrations by angular
orientation intervals but I do not understand why the 0-180
orientation is not vertical by default when using coord_polar().
This is what I do:

require(ggplot2)

#Make example of concentration data (lognormal)
conc <- rnorm(1000,mean=20,sd=5)
conc <- 10^conc
hist(conc)
hist(log10(conc))
#Elements
element <- sample(x=LETTERS[1:3],size=1000,replace=TRUE)
table(element)
#Make distance data
dist <- runif(1000,0.1,50)
#Make orientation data
ang <- rnorm(1000,mean=180,sd=50)
ang[ang<0] <- 0
ang[ang>360] <- 360
hist(ang)
summary(ang)
#Orientation in sectors
angc <- cut(ang,breaks=seq(0,360,by=22.5))
angc3 <- angc
levels(angc3) <- c("(338,22.5]",
                   rep("(22.5,67.5]",2), rep("(67.5,90]",2), rep("(90,135]",2),
                   rep("(135,180]",2),   rep("(180,225]",2), rep("(225,270]",2),
                   rep("(270,338]",2),
                   "(338,22.5]")
df <-data.frame(ID=as.character(1:1000),
                element=element,
                distance=dist,
                angle=ang,
                sector=angc3,
                concentration=conc)

p <- ggplot(data=df) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(x=sector,y=concentration)) +
    scale_y_log10()

p + coord_polar()

As I've been told (In stackoverflow), the next command makes
the 0-180 line be vertical:

p + coord_polar(start=-pi/8)

but would like to understand why this shift is needed: the first interval
is (338,22.5] and has the 0 in the center, thus why 0 is not vertical
by default?

Thanks

messages.subject: Re: color and fill
messages.body_plain:
Agus,

The main problem is that the default plotting shapes for geom_point do not have a "fill" component. If you take a look at ?aes_linetype_size_shape in R or go here <http://docs.ggplot2.org/current/aes_linetype_size_shape.html> for the html version. Looking at the very last example shows that only shapes 21 through 25 take both colour and fill.

To see this try my modifications to your examples

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length)) +

  ggtitle("Iris Data") + geom_point(aes(color=Species),size=5, shape = 21)

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length)) +

  ggtitle("Iris Data") + geom_point(aes(fill = Species), size=5, shape = 21)

After changing the plotting shape to 21, colour changes the borders and fill changes the interior colour, just as you described.

It is also possible to leave the variables mapped to both fill (or colour) and shape simultaneously, but then you'll also need to set the scale manually to shapes that have the additional fill component.

ggplot(iris, aes(x = Petal.Length, y = Sepal.Length)) +

  ggtitle("Iris Data") + geom_point(aes(fill = Species, shape = Species), size=5) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 23, 25))

Thank you for posting a reproducible example.

Jake

messages.subject: Multivariate plots (parallell coordinate or spider / radar plots) i ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate plots (parallell coordinate or spider / radar plots) i ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Am I wrong in thinking that the state of multivariate displays in ggplot2 has worsened?

For parallel coordinate plots, there used to be both the ggpcp and ggparcoord (GGally).

Now:
* ggpcp is deprecated.
* the interface to ggparcoord is confusing and limiting
  - only one grouping column but then the ability to fix that is also limited since other columns appears to be discarded(?) before constructing the ggplot object
  - you have to set an "order", even if the order you want is the order you gave in the columns argument

Spider and radar plots appears to be unwanted citizens in the ggplot2 world.

So, what do you all use for multivariate data?

/Fredrik

messages.subject: Re: Multivariate plots (parallell coordinate or spider / radar plots) i ggplot2
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate plots (parallell coordinate or spider / radar plots) i ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
GGally is the current repository for ggparcoord() and ggfluctuation(),
among others. It is probably the best package for 'multivariate'
graphics using ggplot2. Another option is ggsubplot, where you might
find some support for spider/radar/star plots. Other options are to
search on a topic, e.g. "radar plots ggplot2"; several SO posts have
considered this problem in the past.

It's not that spider and radar plots are "unwanted citizens", but they
just aren't sufficiently unique to warrant inclusion in the package as
a separate geom. There is a post in the issues section of the ggplot2
repo regarding radar plot implementation:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/516. This is what Hadley came
up with; I modified the example a bit to extend it to individual
cases.

library(ggplot2)

# Define a new coordinate system
coord_radar <- function(...) {
  structure(coord_polar(...), class = c("radar", "polar", "coord"))
}
is.linear.radar <- function(coord) TRUE

# rescale all variables to lie between 0 and 1
scaled <- as.data.frame(lapply(mtcars, ggplot2:::rescale01))
scaled$model <- rownames(mtcars)    # add model names as a variable

ggplot(mtcarsm, aes(x = variable, y = value)) +
    geom_path(aes(group = model)) +
    coord_radar() + facet_wrap(~ model) +
    theme(strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.8)),
          axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.8)))

Hadley's solution, then, is to create a new coord_ function, rescale
the variables to be in the same relative coordinates and then use
geom_path() or geom_line() to render the plot. coord_radar() improves
over coord_polar() because the latter turns lines into arcs (remember
that coordinate transformations occur last and have the potential to
alter the configuration of a geom).

The problem is that the polygon does not close. This is fairly easy to
fix in base graphics (add the first element of the input vector to its
end), but is a bit harder to pull off in ggplot2 because the elements
of the polygon are referenced by variable name, which cannot be
duplicated. With a bit of cleverness, one could write a function that
encloses the polygon before rendering it (e.g., add a geom_segment()
to connect the last and first coordinates). Moreover, in combination
with some of the solutions posted on SO in the past, you could
embellish the plot with other features if so desired. I'll leave that
as an exercise :)

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: about adding line equation and object color
messages.subject_clean: about adding line equation and object color
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

(a) Your plot is not reproducible since the rest of us don't know what
is in df1 and df2. If you're using the same variables in both, it may
be simpler to rbind them into one data frame and add a variable with
your two factor labels to distinguish them.
(b) My guess is that if you didn't get the abline, it was because it
was out of the range of your data. Again, we can't tell because the
data are unavailable to anyone but you.
(c) I see no reason why the last line wouldn't work, but to beat a
dead horse, if there is no reproducible example, then one can do
little more than idly speculate.

Here *is* a reproducible example, coded somewhat differently from yours.

df1 <- data.frame(time = seq(10), prod = rnorm(10))
df2 <- data.frame(time = seq(10), prod = rnorm(10, mean = 3))

DF <- rbind(df1, df2)
DF$gp <- factor(rep(c("fact1Prod", "fact2Prod"), each = 10))

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = time, y = prod, color = gp)) +
   geom_point() +
   geom_abline(intercept = -1, slope = 0.2) +
   scale_color_manual("", values = c("red", "blue"))   # correctly ordered

There's nothing wrong with creating factors on the fly with ggplot(),
but sometimes it's just less work to arrange your data in advance so
that the ggplot2 code is simple and straightforward.

Please search on "reproducible example R". When I do this with Google,
the top three hits (StackOverflow, Hadley and R for Dummies) should
all be required reading. Please read and heed in order to make it
easier for others to help you when you have a question.

Dennis

That's actually surprising; I assume it has to do with the oddity of
specifying constant values in an aes() call. The solution is to use
annotate, which is what you want to do in this case anyway:

p + annotate("rect", xmin=2, xmax=10, ymin=0,  ymax=1, fill="black", alpha=0.5)

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Lily, please do read the links Dennis mentioned. We're not being jerks
in harping on the "minimal reproducible example" thing--it really does
make a huge difference, and shows you care about making things easy
for the people trying to help you.

Re your first question, if 'p' is the plot in Dennis's example, then:

p + annotate("text", x=8, y=1, label="y=mb+b")

As to your second question: if your different y's are in different
data frames, then yes, you will need to rbind them together, taking
care to assign some sort of grouping variable if you want to plot them
in different colors (or something like that) later. (I'd recommend
working through, and making sure you understand all of, Dennis's
example.) Another option is to assign the y's to different columns of
a single data frame, and then use reshape2::melt(), or something like
that, to reorganize the data before plotting.

Ben

messages.subject: Calculating the day of the week?
messages.subject_clean: Calculating the day of the week?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I get a daily CSV file that I use to create some descriptive visualizations.

One of the things that I have to do is to modify the date field.  I am currently using the dplyr package with the mutate() function to create a usable date field (YYYY-MM-DD) and a new month number field that I use for a chart.

I am looking for help to figure out how to calculate the day of the week based on the date?  Any tips are appreciated.

==========================
Snippet from my current .R file

require("ggplot2")
require("dplyr")
require("lubridate")

# The raw format of the TimeDate field is: 2015-03-07T00:23:19Z

# use substr() to take positions 1 through 10 of the DateTime field and cut the rest
# assign a date header
df <- mutate(df., date = substr(DateTime,1,10))

# Now my DateTime field is used to create the date filed and it looks like this:  2015-03-07

# add the date field to the dataframe
df$date <- as.Date(df$date)

# using the mutate() function from the dplyr package I get the month numeric.
df <- mutate(df, month=month(date))

messages.subject: Seeking Input on How to Simply Shaping Data for Charts
messages.subject_clean: Seeking Input on How to Simply Shaping Data for Charts
messages.body_plain:
In my R code below I create a summary to narrow the top 10 frequencies in my WatchList field in my dataset.  Then I create a bar chart using my newly shaped data.

I hacked this solution together based on the documentation and it does actually work.

I have to believe there is an easier way to achieve the same results?  The basic idea of shaping data to top 5 or top 10 summaries is something that I will be doing on a regular basis with all sorts of charts (bar, line, histogram, etc).  In many cases, there are too many categories for the frequencies and it makes the charts too busy or just plain messy, thus my solution below to focus on the top 10.

Any thoughts or ideas are appreciated on how to simplify and use for a variety of charts.

=======

mylist.top10 <- names(summary(df.mylist$WatchList, maxsum=10))

ggplot(data=subset(df.mylist,WatchList %in% mylist.top10),
      aes(x=reorder(WatchList, WatchList, length))) +
      geom_bar(stat="bin", fill="#FF3030") +
      labs(title="My Bar Char Title", x="X Label", y="Y Label") +
      coord_flip() +
      theme(panel.grid=element_blank(),
      panel.background=element_blank())

messages.subject_clean: OSX Yosemite - R Studio - ggplot2 won't load - solution
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Excuse this post, I've just started learning about R and had problems installing and running ggplot2 on my Mac.

The long and the short of it is the location of X11. X11 on my Yosemite system is at /opt/X11 - R studio or R or something that lives under the covers is looking for X11 stuff at /usr/X11. I've put in a symlink to fix it (sudo ln -s /opt/X11 /usr/X11) and it all works now, but it should probably be fixed in the code somewhere.

Can you point this at the right people if this isn't the right place to post?

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
I'm writing a plotting function based on ggplot2. The simplification of it is :

myPlot <- function(data, colours = NULL)
{
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = col), data = data) + geom_point() + scale_colour_manual(values = colours)
}

dataFrame <- data.frame(x = 1:3, y = 3:1, col = c('A', 'A', 'B'))

myPlot(dataFrame, c("red", "blue"))  # Works as intended.
myPlot(dataFrame)  # Produces the error.

How can I modify the function to work in both cases ? In the case where colours is NULL, I want the default black points and no legend shown on the right side. The user of my function might only have one category of observations, or they might have more than one. I don't want to write :

myPlot <- function(data, colours = NULL)
{
  if(is.null(colours))
    aPlot <- ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y), data = data)
  else
    aPlot <-ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = col), data = data)

  aPlot <- aPlot + geom_point()

  if(!is.null(colours))
    aPlot <- aPlot + scale_colour_manual(values = colours)
  aPlot
}

This works for both cases, but is untidy.

messages.subject: Re: connecting pairs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam:

You get the vertical lines because geom_line() doesn't adjust for the
dodged points within year. Another approach is to offset the actual
and predicted responses in advance:

library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

actl<-runif(100)
pred<-actl + rnorm(100)
yr<-c(rep(1,50),rep(2,25),rep(3,25))
id <- 1:100

tst <- data.frame(actl,pred,yr,id)
tst.melt<-melt(tst,id.var=c("yr","id"))

# Generate the offset in the data frame
tst.melt$offset <- ifelse(tst.melt$variable == "actl", -0.25, 0.25)

ggplot(tst.melt,aes(yr + offset, value, colour=variable))+
    geom_point() +

messages.body_plain:
Try adding the expand setting for the axes scale functions (scale_x_continuous and scale_y_continuous) --- for example (I’ve split this into separate lines for clarity sake):

ggplot(mtcars) +

geom_point(aes(x = hp, y = wt)) +

geom_vline(xintercept = 150) +

geom_hline(yintercept = 3) +

annotate("rect", xmin = 150, xmax = 340, ymin = 3, ymax = 5.6, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = .3) +

scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0)) +

scale_y_continuous(expand=c(0,0))

This solution is not ideal as the result has a couple of points plotting on the axes, so a KLUDGEd solution to that issue that I came up with is as follows:

x.min <- min(mtcars$hp)

x.min <- x.min - 0.1*x.min

y.min <- min(mtcars$wt)

y.min <- y.min - 0.1*y.min

ggplot(mtcars) +

geom_point(aes(x = hp, y = wt)) +

geom_vline(xintercept = 150) +

geom_hline(yintercept = 3) +

annotate("rect", xmin = 150, xmax = 340, ymin = 3, ymax = 5.6, fill = "darkgreen", alpha = .3) +

scale_x_continuous(limits=c(x.min,340),expand=c(0,0)) +

scale_y_continuous(limits=c(y.min,5.6),expand=c(0,0))

Maybe someone else here will provide a more elegant solution?

Hope this helps-Allen

messages.body_plain:

Adam Loveland

From:        Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com>
To:        adam.l...@pnc.com,
Cc:        ggplot2 <ggp...@googlegroups.com>
Date:        03/13/2015 07:15 PM
Subject:        Re: connecting pairs

Sent by:        ggp...@googlegroups.com

Hi Adam:

You get the vertical lines because geom_line() doesn't adjust for the
dodged points within year. Another approach is to offset the actual
and predicted responses in advance:

library(ggplot2)
library(reshape2)

actl<-runif(100)
pred<-actl + rnorm(100)
yr<-c(rep(1,50),rep(2,25),rep(3,25))
id <- 1:100

tst <- data.frame(actl,pred,yr,id)
tst.melt<-melt(tst,id.var=c("yr","id"))

# Generate the offset in the data frame
tst.melt$offset <- ifelse(tst.melt$variable == "actl", -0.25, 0.25)

ggplot(tst.melt,aes(yr + offset, value, colour=variable))+
   geom_point() +
   geom_line(aes(group=id)) +
   labs(x = "year")

Dennis

Stefan,

The closest I could get to what (I think) you described that you want, is as follows:

ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) +

geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y") +

coord_flip() +

stat_summary(aes(x=factor(cyl +.5)), fun.y=mean, geom = "point", shape = 6, size = 4) +

scale_x_discrete(breaks=seq(4,8,2))

Note three things … (1) I replaced your “fun.y=median” with “fun.y=mean” since you stated you wanted the mean ... not the median; and (2) it doesn’t matter what value you add to “cyl” in the 4th line above … the “shape=6” symbols get plotted half-way between the factored “cyl” values in the original data; and (3) the “scale_x_discrete” needs to added to keep the axis from labelling the “6.5” corresponding ‘factor’.

Not sure if this actually gets you what you want.

Maybe someone else here can suggest something that works more elegantly than my solution.

messages.body_plain:
The plot does not "fail" - the way you've constructed it makes it
impossible to see the result of the last call because the fill color
of points is the same in all three calls. Here's a modified version of
your code; the line is removed to better see what is going on. The
point shape is also changed to unfilled to show that the last call
indeed works.

ggplot(aData, aes(x = C, y = D, colour = A)) +
    geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21)

last_plot() + geom_point(size = 10, shape = 21)
last_plot() + geom_point(size = 2, shape = 21)

As for your original plot, one suggestion is to change to an unfilled
point shape (21-25) as follows:

overlapPlot <- ggplot(aData, aes(x = C, y = D, colour = A, shape = B)) +

                 geom_line(size = 2) + geom_point(size = 3) +
                 scale_shape_manual(values = c(21, 22))

last_plot() + geom_point(size = 10)
last_plot() + geom_point(size = 1)

ggplot2 is based on grid graphics, and grid operates on the "painter's
model" - to quote Paul Murrell in Chapter 5 of R Graphics, 2e:

"Like the traditional system, all grid output occurs on the current
device, and later output obscures any earlier output that it overlaps
(i.e.,output follows the “painters model”)."

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Here's one way:

DF <- read.table(header = TRUE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE, text = "

year    month    day    temp    precip       date
2008      1           1       -10         0.0    2008-01-01
2008      1           2         5          NA    2008-01-02
2008      1           3         2          0.1    2008-01-03
2008      1           4         1          0.2    2008-01-04
2008      1           5         2          0.1    2008-01-05
2008      1           6        -3          0.2    2008-01-06

2008      1           7        -8          NA    2008-01-07")

DF$date <- as.Date(DF$date)

# Find the day of the week and produce an abbreviated day label
library(lubridate)
DF$dow <- wday(DF$date, label = TRUE)

# Use geom_text to position the text
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = day, y = temp)) +
   geom_point(color = "darkorange") +
   geom_text(aes(x = day + 0.1, label = dow), size = 3, hjust = 0)

Dennis

messages.subject: ggplot is varying the stacking order of bars within a single facet
messages.subject_clean: ggplot is varying the stacking order of bars within a single facet
messages.body_plain:
I'm having a weird (to me at least) problem in which ggplot is varying the order in which bars are stacked within a facet. The picture below shows what is going on. Reproducible code follows. In the image below, the bars should be stacked with blue on the bottom, followed by green, followed by red on top (just as in the legend), and most of them are indeed stacked in this order. However, notice in the left facet that the bar at 4.5 years is stacked in a different order, with red on the bottom, followed by green. In the right facet, the bars at 1.5, 2, and 3.5 years are stacked in the wrong order as well. Also note that even though some of the bars are stacked incorrectly, the text values that go with each bar are in the correct locations. The fill variable ("pst.flg" in the code below) is a factor, which should (and in my previous experience does) result in the bars being stacked in order of the factor levels. I can't remember ever seeing variable stacking order within a facet like this.

 <https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-N9OjEEliP-o/VRBqJS5-2II/AAAAAAAAA0U/s2CkJU4mfSg/s1600/Rplot01.png>

Here's the code to reproduce the graph. Data is at the bottom of this message.

ggplot(dat1, aes(years, pct, fill=pst.flg)) +
    geom_bar(stat="identity", colour='grey20', lwd=0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(label=round(pct), y=pct.pos, colour=pst.flg), size=2.5, colour="grey95") +
    facet_grid(coh.termAbbr ~ coh) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks=seq(1,10,1)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks=c(0,50)) +
    labs(fill="", x="Years", y="Percent") +
    scale_fill_manual(name="",breaks=c("Not Enrolled","Enrolled","Graduated"),
                    values=hcl(seq(375,15, length.out=4)[-1], 100, 65))

Another strange thing: If instead of "dat1" I sort the data first (ggplot(dat1 %>% arrange(years, pst.flg), etc.), then all the bars come out stacked in the proper order. This doesn't solve my problem, because in my full data set, using arrange() doesn't solve the stacking problem.

Does anyone have an idea of what could be causing this and how to fix it?

Thanks,
Joel

messages.subject: Re: density strips in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
I'm the author of the denstrip package and associated paper, and came across this old thread while (finally!) learning how to use the excellent ggplot2.   I think ggplot2 can do everything I suggested - I should redo the denstrip documentation to include ggplot2 recipes!

Tom W and others - something like the original attachment can be done as follows: note the use of a "ypos" variable to set the y position of each strip, and the "height" aesthetic for the strip thickness.

x <- seq(-1, 5, by=0.01) # points to evaluate the density at
df2 <- data.frame( x = rep(x, 3),
    dens = c(dnorm(x, 1.25, .35),  dnorm(x, -.5, .15),  dnorm(x,  2, 1)),
    ypos = rep(c(1, 4, 5), each=length(x)))

ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = ypos)) + theme_bw() +
  geom_tile(aes(fill =  dens), height=0.2) +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="white", high="black")

or if you want the maximum density to be black in every strip (see the paper for discussion of this):

df2$maxdens <- rep(with(df2, tapply(dens, factor(ypos, levels=unique(ypos)), max)), each=length(x))
df2$dens.unscaled <- df2$dens / df2$maxdens

ggplot(df2, aes(x = x, y = ypos)) + theme_bw() +
  geom_tile(aes(fill =  dens.unscaled), height=0.2) +
  scale_fill_continuous(low="white", high="black")

If you need to estimate the density from data, then use stat_density(.., geom="tile"), as already suggested.

Aaron - a 2D binhex plot with density strips of the marginal distribution can be done using something like

qplot(x, y, data = diamonds, geom="hex", fill=..density..*10, xlim = c(3, 10),  ylim = c(3, 10), binwidth = c(0.1, 0.1)) + theme_bw() +
        stat_density(aes(y=3.5, fill=..density.., height=0.5), geom="tile", position="identity") +
        stat_ydensity(aes(x=3.5, fill=..density.., width=0.4, height=1), geom="tile", position="identity") +
        scale_fill_continuous(low="white", high="black")

The difficulty here is scaling the densities of the strips and the hexagons so that both go from (roughly) white to black.

Chris

messages.subject: Re: scale_linetype_manual not respecting order of 'values'
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the reproducible example. I believe it's happening because
the 'breaks' are still subject to the default factor ordering, which
is (F, T), which means that solid gets mapped to F and longdash to T.
You can just take out the breaks argument entirely, which is not
needed in this case, to get what you want:

... +   scale_linetype_manual(values=c("solid", "longdash")) + ...

Ben

messages.subject_clean: facets work in qplot but facet_wrap does produces error in ggplot
messages.body_plain:
Hey Loren,
The reason is because ggplot looks for the column names of the data frame you pass into it. In your example, `hetshoms` has columns V1-8. Wayne’s suggestion was to give the data frame legit column names so that it would successfully find the column names of `start`, `HetRatio` and `chrom`.

As for why it works with qplot, read the ?qplot’s `data` argument and that will explain why it worked.

Cheers,
Doug

messages.body_plain:
Allen,

Thanks for your solution sketch (and for pointing out my copy & paste errors)!

Your sketch is close to my intention, but I want the mean values to get binned themselves, ie centred on their corresponding bins.

In the meantime, I came up with the following:

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)) + geom_dotplot(binaxis = "y", binwidth=1)
g <- ggplot_build(p)
mtcars[order(mtcars$cyl),]$bcenter <- g$data[[1]]$y
m$y <- aggregate(mpg ~ cyl, mtcars, function(x) {
    a <- mean(x);
    mtcars$bcenter[which.min(abs(mtcars$bcenter-a))]
})[,2]
p + geom_point(aes (x = factor(cyl + .5), y = y), data = m, color = "red")

In essence, I figured that I can access the plot geometry using ggplot_build to get the computed bin centers (g$data[[1]]$y) and then find the closest matching bin centers for the mean values.

This gives me mean points centred on bins, however, there is a major flaw: Using ggplot_build, I can only access bin centers of actually filled (non-empty) bins. If the mean value would fall into an empty bin range, the above would result in a misleading visualisation :/

Any ideas how to get centers of *all* (empty and non-empty) bins?

Cheers,
Stefan

messages.subject: Re: Adjust vertically two ggplots
messages.body_plain:
Hi you could use the following function to align your y axis on both the plots.

> library(ggplot2)
> library(grid)
> library(gridExtra)
> align_plots <- function (...)
> {
>   pl <- list(...)
>   stopifnot(do.call(all, lapply(pl, inherits, "gg")))
>   gl <- lapply(pl, ggplotGrob)
>   bind2 <- function(x, y) gtable:::rbind_gtable(x, y, "first")
>   combined <- Reduce(bind2, gl[-1], gl[[1]])
>   wl <- lapply(gl, "[[", "widths")
>   combined$widths <- do.call(grid::unit.pmax, wl)
>   grid::grid.newpage()
>   grid::grid.draw(combined)
> }

To verify, just test with following code:

> align_plots(qplot(1,1),qplot(100,100),qplot(1000,1000)+ylab("two \n lines"))

ps: I found this code on internet some time back but couldn't find it now to give appropriate credit.

Hope it helps.

Janesh Devkota

messages.subject: Re: error bars not dodged
messages.body_plain:
Hi Felix,

I've come across this too. I'm not sure why, but adding `fill = Group` to the mapping for the error bars will fix the dodging. Maybe one of the experts can chime in as to why this is the case, but meanwhile here's one possibility, using your 'y' data.frame:

library(ggplot2)
library(plyr)

# map the levels of y$Group
y$Group <- mapvalues(y$Group, from = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"),
                     to = c("1:atAlHV-1 + Em", "2:atAlHV-1 + Fli-C", "3:atAlHV-1 + \nEm + Fli-C", "4:Em", "5:Fli-C"))

# set the position dodge
pd <- position_dodge(2)

g <- ggplot(y, aes(x = week, y = titre_2_AnnNS_T2)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Group), stat = 'identity', position = pd) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(fill = Group, ymin=titre_2_AnnNS_T2-se, ymax=titre_2_AnnNS_T2+se),
                position = pd, width = 0.4, size = 0.3) +
  facet_grid(sample ~., scales ="free") +

  xlab("Week") + ylab("1 / titre")

# create df for annotation text
nd <- data.frame(week = c(0, 4, 11),
                 titre_2_AnnNS_T2=c(90, 90, 90),
                 sample=factor(c("Neut-NS"), levels = levels(y$sample)),
                 Text=c("P", "B", "C"))

g + geom_text(aes(x = week, y = titre_2_AnnNS_T2, label = Text), size = 2, data=nd)

I used plyr to rename the factor levels in Group but your way with `scale_fill_discrete` works too.

Cheers,

Tom

messages.subject: Workaround for geom_contour and not perfectly gridded data?
messages.subject_clean: Workaround for geom_contour and not perfectly gridded data?
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to plot an overlay onto ggmaps that I'm hoping to construct a heatmap out of. The data is Lat/Long locations, plus an additional value z. I am trying to visualize any spatial gradient of Z.I know there are better tools for this, but I wanted to get a cursory look using ggmaps. Unfortunately, it seems as though the existing functions I can find (geom_contour()) for ggmaps do not allow for the data to be anything but a perfect grid.

Is there any good way to interpolate between irregular sites with this sort of data?

Thank you!

Best wishes,

Felix

On 29 Mar 2015, at 16:01, Tom Harrop <twha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Felix,
>
> I've come across this too. I'm not sure why, but adding `fill = Group` to the mapping for the error bars will fix the dodging. Maybe one of the experts can chime in as to why this is the case, but meanwhile here's one possibility, using your 'y' data.frame:
>
> library(ggplot2)
> library(plyr)
>
>
> # map the levels of y$Group
> y$Group <- mapvalues(y$Group, from = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5"),
>                      to = c("1:atAlHV-1 + Em", "2:atAlHV-1 + Fli-C", "3:atAlHV-1 + \nEm + Fli-C", "4:Em", "5:Fli-C"))
>
>
> # set the position dodge
> pd <- position_dodge(2)
>
>
> g <- ggplot(y, aes(x = week, y = titre_2_AnnNS_T2)) +
>   geom_bar(aes(fill = Group), stat = 'identity', position = pd) +
>   geom_errorbar(aes(fill = Group, ymin=titre_2_AnnNS_T2-se, ymax=titre_2_AnnNS_T2+se),
>                 position = pd, width = 0.4, size = 0.3) +
>   facet_grid(sample ~., scales ="free") +
>   xlab("Week") + ylab("1 / titre")
>
>
> # create df for annotation text
> nd <- data.frame(week = c(0, 4, 11),
>                  titre_2_AnnNS_T2=c(90, 90, 90),
>                  sample=factor(c("Neut-NS"), levels = levels(y$sample)),
>                  Text=c("P", "B", "C"))
>
>
> g + geom_text(aes(x = week, y = titre_2_AnnNS_T2, label = Text), size = 2, data=nd)
>
> I used plyr to rename the factor levels in Group but your way with `scale_fill_discrete` works too.
>
> Cheers,
>
> Tom
